LETTERS TO THE EDITOR

# Letter: The intersection of CHIP and HIV: Implications for cardiovascular risk stratification

To the Editor: We read with interest the article by Oren and colleagues1 highlighting the association between clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and increased cardiovascular risk and its rel­ evance to internal medicine practice. Expanding this discussion, we would like to describe the interactions between CHIP and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and their implications for internal medicine practice in settings where internists with HIV training often serve as primary care clinicians for people with HIV. People with HIV experience disproportionately high cardiovascular risk driven by chronic immune activation, persistent inflammation, antiretroviral therapy–associated metabolic effects, higher smoking prevalence, and traditional atherosclerotic risk fac­ tors. Emerging evidence suggests that CHIP is about twice as prevalent in people with HIV compared with HIV-negative individuals and may further amplify this risk burden.2 CHIP, particularly involving TET2 and DNMT3A mutations, contributes to clonal expansion of proinflammatory myeloid cells and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, increasing interleu­ kin-1beta and interleukin-6 signaling and accelerating atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction risk, and mortal­ ity.2,3 CHIP also confers increased risk of hematologic malignancy, compounding long-term morbidity in this aging population. Thus, there is a need for dedicated screening and optimal treatment interventions.2,3 REPRIEVE (Randomized Trial to Prevent Vascu­ lar Events in HIV)2 demonstrated that pitavastatin reduces major adverse cardiovascular events in in­ dividuals with HIV with low-to-moderate tradition­ al risk, reinforcing the importance of early preven­ tive strategies. Although CHIP was not assessed in REPRIEVE, these findings raise the possibility that unmeasured inflammatory drivers such as CHIP may help identify patients who could benefit from earlier or more intensive intervention. CHIP remains underrecognized in HIV care, par­ ticularly among infectious diseases physicians who fre­ quently provide primary care for people with HIV. We agree with Oren and colleagues1 that comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment is essential and propose CHIP as an emerging risk modifier in people with HIV.

Prospective studies are needed to guide screening and targeted interventions in this population.

Abigail Martinez, MD Florida International University, Miami, FL

doi:10.3949/ccjm.93c.08001 In Reply: The intersection of CHIP and HIV: Implications for cardiovascular risk stratification

In Reply: We thank Dr. Martinez and colleagues for their comment on the intersection between clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and cardiovascular risk in people with human immu­ nodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. We would like to shed light on recent data that may further inform this discussion. Since the REPRIEVE (Randomized Trial to Pre­ vent Vascular Events in HIV) trial was completed, Xue et al1 reported the results of a dedicated CHIP analy­ sis in 4,490 REPRIEVE participants using high-depth targeted sequencing. While CHIP overall was not associated with major adverse cardiovascular events, larger CHIP clones (variant allele fraction ≥ 10%) were associated with substantially higher odds of major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial infarction, and coronary revascularization.1 Intriguingly, these as­ sociations persisted despite pitavastatin therapy, sug­ gesting that a component of residual cardiovascular risk in people with HIV may be driven by mechanisms beyond reductions in low-density lipoprotein choles­ terol, potentially involving NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream interleukin-1beta and interleukin-6 signaling.

These findings have broader implications across chronic inflammatory disorders. Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis, gout, and VEXAS (vac­ uoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somat­ ic) syndrome are characterized by excess cardiovascular risk that is not fully explained by traditional risk factors, and have also been associated with increased preva­ lence of CHIP (see supplementary Figure 1 in the PDF version of this article).2–5 Chronic inflammatory signal­ ing may promote clonal expansion, while CHIP-asso­ ciated clones further amplify inflammation, creating a potentially self-reinforcing cycle and contributing to accelerated atherogenesis and the development of in­ flammatory cardiac conditions. In this context, CHIP may not only serve as a biomarker of cardiovascular risk but also as a tool for identifying patients most likely to benefit from approved and emerging anti-inflammatory therapies (supplementary Figure 1). Prospective studies in­ corporating CHIP assessment into cohorts of persons with HIV infection and other inflammatory disease will be important to accurately define its role in risk stratification, therapeutic selection, and precision cardiovascular prevention. The results of ongoing phase 3 trials evaluating interleukin-6 inhibition (ie, ZEUS [Effects of Ziltivekimab Versus Placebo on Cardiovascular Outcomes in Participants With Established Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease and Systemic Inflammation] and ARTEMIS [Effects of Ziltivekimab Versus Pla­ cebo on Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction]) may help define the role of targeted anti-inflammatory therapy in preci­ sion cardiovascular prevention.

doi:10.3949/ccjm.93c.08002 Letter: Olanzapine in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies

To the Editor: We read with interest the recent com­ mentary by Dr. Hao and colleagues1 on the risk of QTc-interval prolongation associated with phar­ macologic management of hyperactive delirium in hospitalized older adults. We agree that the available evidence regarding pharmacologic treatment in this context is limited. However, we believe that certain issues warrant clarification. Among the treatment options for agitation or psy­ chosis, the algorithm presented in Figure 1 includes both quetiapine and olanzapine for patients with Par­ kinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies.1 This presentation may be interpreted as suggesting that both drugs are appropriate and equivalent alterna­ tives. Although robust efficacy data for antipsychotics in this setting remain limited, quetiapine is generally considered the antipsychotic agent of choice in pa­ tients with Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, because it causes fewer extrapyramidal side effects.2 The National Institute for Health and Care Ex­ cellence specifically recommends against the use of olanzapine for managing hallucinations or delusions in people with Parkinson disease.3 Olanzapine has not shown meaningful benefit for psychotic symptoms and has been associated with worse motor function
